The Longspine thornyhead Sebastolobus altivelis displays life history traits shaped by the cold, deep waters of the North Pacific. Field surveys indicate that individuals attain a maximum total length of 39 centimeters [Li = 39 centimeters], a size that positions this species among the larger-bodied scorpionfishes inhabiting continental slope environments. The period of rapid somatic growth characteristic of the juvenile phase transitions gradually into reproductive maturity as fish approach a total length of 27 centimeters [Lp = 27 centimeters], the size at which puberty is typically reached. This length at sexual maturation corresponds to a wet weight of approximately 241 grams [Wwp = approximately 241 grams] according to length-weight regressions derived from trawl-caught specimens. The pronounced investment in somatic growth before gonadal activation appears to be an adaptation to the low and unpredictable food availability that characterizes the benthic habitat at depths exceeding 500 meters.

Egg development in Longspine thornyhead proceeds slowly under the persistently cold conditions of their environment. Individual fertilised ova have a wet weight of 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams] shortly after spawning, a value consistent with the measured egg diameter of 0.8 millimeters observed in gravid females. Pelagic eggs are released during a protracted spawning season, and the endotrophic larvae that emerge depend entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The maximum adult wet weight recorded for this species, based on the length-weight relationship observed in the population, is 752 grams [Wwi = 752 grams], attained as individuals approach their asymptotic length. These substantial body masses reflect the energy-demanding process of building and maintaining large lipid reserves that sustain the fish through extended periods of scarce prey.

Reproductive output in Sebastolobus altivelis is tightly coupled to the thermal regime of the deep sea. Under laboratory conditions designed to mimic the ambient temperature of their natural habitat at 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C], females produce approximately 137 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 137 eggs per day], reflecting a reproductive strategy that maximizes annual output in a cold, low-productivity environment. This daily rate underscores the species' capacity for substantial gamete production despite the energetic constraints of deep-sea life, and it stands in contrast to the modest fecundity per event observed in many shallow-water scorpaenids. The combination of a protracted spawning season and a slow metabolic pace allows individuals to sustain this output over many years, contributing to the species' overall reproductive success in an environment where recruitment opportunities are sporadic.

Longevity represents a defining characteristic of this species life history. Mark-recapture studies and otolith-based ageing have documented a maximum lifespan of 45 years [am = 45 years] for individuals inhabiting waters at 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C]. This extreme longevity, exceeding that of most sympatric scorpionfishes, is facilitated by a slow metabolic pace and the low ambient temperatures that reduce rates of cellular aging. The combination of delayed maturation, modest annual fecundity, and an extended adult life span positions the Longspine thornyhead as a classic K-selected strategist among marine fishes. Reliable age estimation from otolith thin sections has proven critical for validating these life span data, as growth increments are narrowly spaced in older individuals.

The physiological ecology of Sebastolobus altivelis is further illuminated by considering the interplay between growth and reproduction. The ultimate size of this species, defined by a total length of 39 centimeters [Li = 39 centimeters], is attained after many decades of slow, sustained growth. Fish reaching the pubertal length of 27 centimeters [Lp = 27 centimeters] have likely invested 15 to 20 years in somatic development before diverting resources toward gamete production. The substantial post-maturation growth—from approximately 241 grams [Wwp = approximately 241 grams] at puberty to 752 grams [Wwi = 752 grams] in fully grown adults—highlights the extreme size disparity between the earliest life stage at 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams] and the reproductively active adult, a pattern consistent with other deep-sea scorpaenids.
